params.question: Which set of clinical findings at presentation is used to classify the type of abortion, even before ultrasonography is available?

answers.text: Serum beta-hCG level, gestational age, fetal heart rate, and amniotic fluid volume

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: These are laboratory and ultrasound parameters, not bedside clinical anchors. Beta-hCG and ultrasound help assess viability, but the type of abortion is classified using findings obtainable on clinical examination alone.

answers.text: Cervical os status, uterine size for dates, whether tissue has been passed, and presence of infection

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. These four bedside clinical anchors — open or closed os, uterine size appropriate or small for dates, partial or complete tissue expulsion, and signs of infection — allow classification into threatened, inevitable, incomplete, complete, missed, or septic abortion without imaging.

answers.text: Maternal blood group, coagulation profile, cervical length, and volume of bleeding

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Blood group and coagulation studies are important for management (anti-D prophylaxis, DIC screening) but are not the clinical anchors used to classify the type of abortion at the bedside.

answers.text: Progesterone level, beta-hCG doubling time, endometrial thickness, and pain severity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Beta-hCG doubling time and progesterone help assess viability and ectopic risk, but classifying the type of abortion rests on four bedside clinical anchors, not on laboratory or ultrasound values.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the four clinical anchors: (1) cervical os open or closed, (2) uterine size appropriate for dates, (3) whether tissue has been passed, and (4) presence of infection. These allow bedside classification of the abortion type.
The four clinical anchors — cervical os status, uterine size, tissue passage, and presence of infection — are the foundation of abortion classification, usable at the bedside even before ultrasound.

interactions.label: Both the RCOG and the ASRM define recurrent pregnancy loss as three or more cons

params.question: Both the RCOG and the ASRM define recurrent pregnancy loss as three or more consecutive pregnancy losses before 20 weeks of gestation.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is false. While RCOG and ESHRE define RPL as three or more consecutive losses before 20 weeks, the ASRM uses a lower threshold of two or more ultrasound-confirmed losses. For NMC examinations, know both definitions and state which one you are using.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. The RCOG and ESHRE define RPL as three or more consecutive losses before 20 weeks, but the ASRM uses a less stringent threshold of two or more ultrasound-confirmed clinical losses, recognising that even two losses warrant investigation given the emotional burden and likelihood of finding a treatable cause.

interactions.label: Which clinical finding is described as pathognomonic for a complete hydatidiform

params.question: Which clinical finding is described as pathognomonic for a complete hydatidiform mole?

answers.text: Uterus larger than expected for the period of gestation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A large-for-dates uterus is characteristic of complete mole but is not pathognomonic — it can also occur in multiple pregnancy, polyhydramnios, or incorrect dating.

answers.text: Continuous dark vaginal bleeding in the first trimester

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Moderate to heavy first-trimester bleeding is common in complete mole but has many other causes (threatened abortion, ectopic pregnancy) and is not pathognomonic for gestational trophoblastic disease.

Correct. The passage of grape-like vesicles — swollen chorionic villi — is pathognomonic for hydatidiform mole. When seen clinically, it confirms the diagnosis even before histopathological examination.

Theca-lutein cysts result from markedly elevated beta-hCG stimulating the ovaries and are associated with complete mole, but they are not pathognomonic — they can occur in any condition with very high hCG levels, including multiple pregnancy.

overallFeedback.feedback: While bleeding and a large-for-dates uterus are characteristic, only the passage of grape-like (hydatid) vesicles is pathognomonic for molar pregnancy — no other condition produces this finding.
Grape-like vesicles are pathognomonic for hydatidiform mole. Their passage per vaginum alongside vaginal bleeding and a large-for-dates uterus makes the diagnosis clinically certain.

params.question: After suction evacuation for an incomplete abortion, which confirmatory step provides the structural proof that pregnancy tissue has been successfully removed?

answers.text: Noting that the uterine cavity felt empty and gritty during the procedure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The intraoperative tactile 'gritty feel' suggests adequate curettage, but it is a subjective assessment and does not provide structural confirmation that products of conception were actually retrieved.

answers.text: Observing a significant reduction in vaginal bleeding within 30 minutes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Reduced bleeding is reassuring but does not confirm that all products of conception have been removed. Retained tissue can initially cause minimal bleeding but later lead to haemorrhage or sepsis.

answers.text: Visual inspection of the aspirated tissue to identify chorionic villi

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Identifying chorionic villi in the aspirated tissue is the structural proof that pregnancy tissue has been removed. This inspection must be performed in the procedure room before the patient is discharged.

answers.text: Confirming a falling serum beta-hCG level at 48-hour follow-up

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A falling beta-hCG confirms resolution over time, but it is a delayed test. Confirmation that evacuation is complete must occur in the procedure room — before discharge — to prevent complications from retained products.

overallFeedback.feedback: The structural proof of successful evacuation is visual identification of chorionic villi in the aspirated tissue. The three confirmatory steps are: (1) intraoperative tactile assessment, (2) visual inspection for villi, and (3) ultrasound where available.
Identifying chorionic villi in the aspirated tissue is the definitive in-procedure confirmation of successful evacuation — it must be done before the patient leaves the procedure room.
